messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was seventy-nine years old when he finally walked into a clinic, a wiry man whose hands had spent decades stacking boxes in a warehouse, and whose mind had spent far longer trying to outrun a single night. He was born in a small village in Ghana, and when he was seven years old, he had watched his father beat his mother until she stopped moving. He could not remember the sound of her voice that night, or the color of the dress she wore. What he remembered, or rather what he felt, was a terror that arrived without warning, without an image attached, like a wave that knocked the air from his lungs. When he tried to recall the event deliberately, the pieces would not fit together—a shard of moonlight through a window, the smell of palm wine on his father’s breath, the thud of a body hitting packed earth—but no whole story, no sequence. He had learned not to try.

For decades, Kwame had managed by keeping himself surrounded. He worked double shifts, stayed late to help unload trucks, and then drove straight to a friend’s house or a bar where he knew people. He kept himself constantly surrounded by people so that he was never alone with his thoughts. The quiet of his own apartment was unbearable; there, the emotion without image would rise up, and he would feel the full intensity of that childhood terror as if it were happening, even though he could see nothing. So he avoided quiet. He avoided nature, too—parks, wooded trails, even the small garden behind his building—because the stillness of trees and open air reminded him of the field behind his family’s compound where he had run that night, hiding until dawn. More than anything, he avoided the smell of alcohol. A coworker’s beer at a warehouse barbecue, a stranger’s breath on the bus—these could send him into a cold sweat, his chest tightening, his hands shaking.

When the smell hit him, or when a door slammed in the warehouse office and the sound cracked through him like a whip, Kwame’s first instinct was to drown it. He drank alcohol, took medication he bought from a friend, or used whatever he could find to blunt the edge. The drinking did not stop the memories, though; it loosened them, and late at night, after a few beers, the fragmented pieces would surface more vividly, the disconnected images spinning faster. He had come to believe that if he stopped moving, if he stopped drinking, the terror would swallow him whole. So he picked arguments, too. He would snap at a coworker over a misplaced pallet, or start a fight with his ex-wife on the phone over nothing, because the rush of anger was simpler than the rush of fear. The conflict distracted him, gave him something to hold onto, but it also left him isolated. His children stopped calling as often. His supervisor put him on warning.

The cycle tightened over the months. A door slamming at work would trigger a surge of fear, and Kwame would head to the bar after his shift, drinking until the edges softened. But the drinking made the memory more intrusive, and the next morning he would be raw and irritable, picking a fight with anyone nearby, which in turn kept him out of the warehouse—avoiding the triggers he knew were waiting. He had come to believe that he was weak, that other men had survived worse and moved on, and that his inability to let go of a childhood night meant something was fundamentally broken in him. What frightened him most was the feeling itself: the terror without a picture, the way his body could be hijacked by something he could not even see.

What finally brought Kwame to the clinic was his supervisor’s ultimatum—one more incident, and he was out—and the quiet realization that he had spent seventy-nine years running from a night he could not even properly remember. He sat in the intake chair, his hands on his knees, and said, “I just want to stop feeling it. I don’t even know what I’m afraid of anymore.”
